title: A pullet's first eggs are smaller and rounder than its later ones

fields.label: Label
fields.value: A pullet's first eggs are smaller and rounder than its later ones

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In the domestic fowl egg size and shape are directly related: a young pullet's first eggs are smaller and more nearly spherical than later ones, and breeds laying relatively smaller eggs lay rounder eggs.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In the case of the common fowl we can trace a direct relation between the size and shape of the egg, for the first eggs laid by a young pullet are usually smaller, and at the same time are much more nearly spherical than the later ones

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XV, “On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures”; topic “Egg size and asymmetry”. Scope: domestic fowl (Gallus gallus domesticus)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch15-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The within-individual prediction is direct and highly discriminating. Existing public records likely test subsets, but a dataset jointly containing laying sequence, size and shape across breeds is not assured.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Analyze hen-level longitudinal laying records with egg mass and shape index, testing whether first eggs are smaller and rounder than later eggs and whether breeds with smaller relative eggs have rounder shapes. Consistent within-hen trajectories and breed effects support the claim; absent or reversed effects refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Public poultry datasets often omit egg shape or exact laying order.

Feed, age, housing and selection line confound breed comparisons.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The within-bird and among-breed comparisons are precise and, for domestic fowl, match the claim's scope exactly. The large avian datasets do not resolve a pullet's laying sequence or breed differences, so the needed numbers are scattered in the poultry literature rather than sitting in one open file. Discrimination would be high after a compilation, which is why the claim is only partly resolvable from what is already released.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Within domestic fowl, compare egg mass and a roundness index between a pullet's first eggs and her later eggs, and among breeds that differ in relative egg size. The claim is confirmed if first eggs are both smaller and rounder, and if breeds laying smaller eggs relative to body size lay rounder ones; either association failing would refute the corresponding half.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Cross-species egg tables collapse Gallus to a single average and omit laying sequence.

Breed and age series exist mainly as tables inside poultry papers and would have to be compiled.
